And that gives you that vibrancy and energy and tension and acidity that I think makes this wine so endearing.

RG

So let’s say I’m I’m I’m in the U.S., I listen to this podcast, I’m completely Bardolino pilled, I’m on board. What are one or two producers I should be looking for if I want to pick up a bottle?

JP

So there are two producers I really love. Both of them farm certified organic with biodynamic practices. One’s called Le Fraghe. That is a historic estate that just makes these wines of so much elegance, beauty, and the wines taste as they should. They are, if you want to know what the place tastes like, that’s the one to start with. And there’s another producer named Gorgo, G-O-R-G-O, Gorgo. And she also produces wines in a similar style.

But with a little more kind of richness on the back end of the palate. But both wines are absolutely bangers.

RG

What’s the price point on these?

JP

They’re like in the twenties, mid twenties.

RG

Sounds good to me.

JP

Yeah, the the QPR on these wines is super high.

RG

Now, are you seeing more and more of these in restaurants, or are they kind of slowly popping up in restaurants in the U.S.?

JP

You know, I think it’s a slow burn. If you’re in a place with a restaurant list that is primarily or almost all Italian, you’ll definitely find some. But you know, there are some new producers coming on board that got picked up recently by some energetic young importers in the United States. So I think you’ll start to see it because there’s another generation of producers is starting to take over in the region, and they’re more savvy at social media and projecting their stories out there.

So they’re putting more noise out there and getting more feedback, which is good.

RG

Thanks so much for being here. This has been great.

JP

No, no, my pleasure. Thank you very much. I could talk about Bardolino and drink it with you for a long time.

RG

All right, well maybe we’ll do a Bardolino only episode in the future. But for now, we got two more regions to talk about.

RG

And now we’re gonna travel south with Writer at Large Danielle Callegari, who’s hopping on to talk about the Maremma, a subregion of Tuscany.

RG

Hey Danielle, thanks so much for being here.

Danielle Callegari

Thank you for having me, it’s a pleasure.

RG

So we’re here to talk about the Maremma in Tuscany. Why do you think the Maremma is a little underappreciated?

DC

So there are few practical reasons that have led the Maremma to be less loved than other parts of Tuscany. One is that historically it was a swamp that had to be, as the Italians refer to it, requalified. So under Mussolini’s fascist regime, they came in and filled in a lot of the swampy areas and made it much more practical for farming and all kinds of agriculture in general. And so it’s, you know, as far as Italy is concerned, a relatively young region for agriculture. It’s also because of its location. It’s not on the kind of Grand Tour trail. So when you’re coming up from Rome, you shoot inwards towards Florence and you kind of skip the Maremma altogether. 

And again, because of the fact that it wasn’t as easy to work with, it didn’t have great infrastructure and wasn’t easy to get to. So, you know, people kind of just ran right past it, I guess you could say, for a lot of the last century. And then there’s I think a side to it that’s sort of a culture of this particular subzone of Tuscany where the people who live there kind of like that they’re a little bit off map, and they’ve been protective of that space. And one can easily understand that when you see the way Florence has become over the last decade or so.

RG

Yeah, so you see it referred to as the wild west of Tuscany. That kind of plays into that sort of like off-the-beaten-path sort of mentality.

DC

Yeah, it is, I think. It’s something that is a reality of its geographic position, but also a theme that the people who live there have leaned into. I think in the article that I wrote for our Italy issue this year on the Maremma, I said that I think of it more as like the Amazon than the Wild West. And

I stand by that because I don’t know that the ranching part of it is the thing that makes it as wild or difficult to connect with as its incredible lush mountainsides and forests and the kind of density of biodiversity that’s there that roll right up onto the coast. And in fact recently I’ve been kind of anecdotally asking people in America if they even realize that Tuscany has a coast. It’s not the kind of Tuscany we think of, either way. 

So, you know, when you think of Under the Tuscan Sun, you think of the villas and the countryside, rolling hills, lots of vineyards, a lot of land planted to vine. You think of Renaissance art, you think of palaces, you think of medieval towns that are then built out into kind of Renaissance splendor.

And we don’t think of Tuscany as a place where there are cliffs and sea and there are lush forests exactly. So it also doesn’t dovetail with expectations, and that makes it exciting to me, but it does also make it a little bit harder for people to access, I think, even just in their mind.

RG

Yeah, and when what’s the sea imparting on the wines there? How are these wines in Maremma different than what you would think of as a Tuscan wine?

DC

Yeah, I think so. I do think that that’s something to to spend time on when you’re considering what distinguishes wines from this particular area, the salt air and the shells that are in the soil, which we know, I mean that’s true of a lot of Tuscany, but in this area there’s an incredible salinity of freshness, of course.

But one thing that I found, especially talking more attentively with my my friends who make wine around there, thinking about it for for this issue and and for this article in particular, that they kept pointing out to me was the presence of a kind of consistent wind and that cooling effect that comes off of the water that unites them with other coastal regions that people are more familiar with, like Bolgheri and Suvereto, which is not particularly famous, but that I think has been appreciated a little bit more. The entire coast of Tuscany has this very different climate because of the sea air that’s there, not just for the salty part, which people are really into right now and is kind of a hip buzzy wine word, but also again, right, because of that wind. 

So if we’re thinking, for example, this July where a lot of Tuscany has seen multiple days that are over a hundred degrees, or even over a hundred and five degrees Fahrenheit, the coast is is hot still, but they have this persistent cooling effect from the wind that keeps them in a kind of very different growth cycle than a lot of the rest of the region.

RG

Yeah, and your story talks a lot about the kind of youthful energy there and the experimentation going on. Who are some of these major players that are kind of changing things up in the region?

DC

I would say that generally I’d really emphasize that the best thing about that or the thing that Maremma most has going for it is this lack of attention, because you go to you know Brunello, you go to Montalcino, you go to Chianti, there’s a lot of history and that also means a lot of baggage, a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure. 

So while in all the other parts of Tuscany there are plenty of young people jumping in and taking over their family properties, or beginning to work together with the older generation, they have to work, you know, inside of certain parameters. With boundaries and guardrails up for sure. And you go to the Maremma, and because there aren’t expectations and there isn’t an already kind of cemented relationship with a certain audience, there’s just a lot more experimentation all around. And I started really paying attention seriously to the area. When I first visited Tancredi Biondi Santi’s property, Castello di Montepò, not least because, as his name announces, there’s a lot of history in his family when it comes to winemaking. And so when I found out that he was working in this other very different space, I was of course already kind of curious, just

in a very general way, what brought someone who had been making wine in the most famous part of Tuscany in the most famous house, probably in all of Italy for a long time, to choose this area and what was he up to? 

It’s not just that he happened to come across this property. It’s something he really believes in. And so when I saw his enthusiasm and excitement about this particular territory, I decided that it was worth digging into. And then right near him is one of my other favorite properties in the area, Fattoria Le Pupille, first made famous a long time ago by Elisabetta Geppetti, who is a woman who absolutely embodies great choices, I think. She’s somebody who’s just tasteful in every way, and her wines always reflect that. And she turned over, much to her credit, she turned over winemaking to her very young son, Ettore, and she remains extremely active in property. 

But I think I understood that the strength of this region was the fact that there were young people here and that they were able to be playful and figure out what was best for them. And Ettore makes really, really elegant wines, but also really unexpected ones. I really fell in love first with the Petit Manseng that he makes, which is to me an icon of this area because it is so unexpected. You’re not going to Tuscany looking for Petit Manseng, obviously. You’re not expecting to find a cru or a clos, in this case, of any white wines really and you’re not expecting to find somebody who really kind of lets it be what it’s going to be without kind of trying to shoehorn it into some predisposed idea and that you know, when I come back to that wine, from Fattoria Le Pupille, I always say to myself, you know, this is like the reward you get for being a little bit intrepid.

RG

So, it’s almost like the lack of the anxiety of influence is one of their greatest sort of, you know, benefits of the region, right?

DC

Hundred percent. And as a literature professor first and foremost, nothing makes me happier than being able to cite Harold Bloom in the course of a podcast.

RG

What are they growing up there other than Sangiovese and Petit Manseng?

DC

Well, there’s really everything. Speaking of people experimenting. And I think, you know, one of the things that’s a challenge for the region right now is trying to get a more coherent identity. So all that experimentation can become a little bit chaotic, even though I find that to be very fun. On the other hand, one thing that you can definitely look for and always find, and that does I think have a kind of a real clarity of vision is their Vermentino. And that’s, as you expect, it’s exactly the kind of grape that will do well under these circumstances. And I think that almost every producer… I just did a big tasting for them. It went along with the writing that I was doing for the magazine at the same time. And I found that the Vermentinos were really where everyone was not necessarily making a showstopper, but was making something super reliable, really delicious, and extremely accessible to almost any consumer, certainly this time of year, a Vermentino is, you know, warm citrus, a little salt, a nice high acid, exactly what you’re looking for in on on a summer afternoon. 

And then from there you can get into all kinds of really special expressions of the so-called international varietals, plenty of people working with Cabernet and Merlot and then you have everything in between. And of course the Sangiovese from the area that’s known colloquially as Morellino is something that has had mixed fortunes. It got really popular for a little while, then it kind of lost some of that traction. But now I think it’s very well positioned because it’s the kind of leaner, fresher, crunchier version of Sangiovese that right now audiences seem to really find themselves in.

RG

In the U.S. at least, what do you think the future holds? Because I know that some of these are pretty reasonably priced wines, what’s their their strategy? Like what are they looking forward to?

DC

I think if they do it right, they can take advantage of the thing that I’m always trying to push, especially Italian producers to really understand, which is that the American audience is without preconceptions. So while Italians see these things about the different regions, either on a grand scale from Tuscany to Piedmont or in a more zoomed in lens, looking at the difference between, for example, Brunello di Montalcino and coastal Tuscany. There they have these understandings of the long history of how wine was produced, of what people expect to have from those areas and whether or not they esteem them because of that. Whereas Americans, of course, are not held back by any of that. So these would be kind of new regions or less loved ones have an opportunity to connect with new incoming drinkers, whatever age they are, who are just finding what they like for the first time. And at the super accessible price point they feel comfortable experimenting and taking a risk. And I think they’ll be delighted with what they find.

RG

Well I think that about covers it. I think we did it. Thanks so much for being here.

DC

It’s been a pleasure as usual, Ryan. Thank you.

RG

So we saved probably the least well known subregion for last, Mamoiada. Writer at large Michael Laudenslager is on the line to talk about this slice of Sardinia.

RG

Hey Michael, thanks for being here. How’s it going?

Michael Laudenslager

Good, Ryan. What’s going on, man? Thanks for having me.

RG

Good. Yeah, we’re here to talk about Mamoiada. Why do you think Mamoiada is underrated, a little underappreciated?

ML

You know what? Because it started as a wine that was really big, macho, high alcohol. You know, the best way to put it for people to understand is like old man wine, you know what I mean? And that’s pretty much who was making those wines for generations. 

RG

Yeah, and where is it in Sardinia and what’s the landscape?

ML

So you’re pretty much smack in the middle of Sardinia, shaded a little to the east pretty much looking at Tuscany. When you’re thinking of Sardinia, I guess everyone’s thinking of beaches, right? The beautiful south is Cagliari and then the Alghero in the north which is like, you know, billionaires and yacht clubs, right?

We’re in the mountains now. Probably not a lot of tourists have been there. It gets pretty high elevation up there too, which we all know high elevation in wine usually leads to a beautiful thing. You get high acidity and a little bit more precision in those wines. And yeah, they’re making some beautiful Grenache or you know, in that region they call it Cannonau.

RG

Yeah, so you wouldn’t call it a touristy area, but a lot of the wineries, you know, they’re accepting visitors and it’s touristy in its own way, or is it kind of too off the beaten path?

ML

Yeah, it’s really off the beaten path. Like when I stayed there, right after VinItaly, I scheduled a trip to go hang with all these winemakers. And there’s not even a hotel. You know, I try to Airbnb, I think there was one. So one of the winemakers, Simone, who’s became a good friend of mine, let me sleep at one of his buddies’ houses, which was pretty cool.

Yeah, there’s really no tourist attraction there. There’s like maybe a couple restaurants, but really what I found is like one restaurant everyone goes to and just so happens that restaurant owner, the husband and wife, make wine for Mamoiada. And then there’s like one enoteca, which is you know, a wine bar, that guy also makes wine for Mamoiada. It’s really cool. It’s like a whole community dedicated to this group of winemakers called the Mamoja.

RG

How much of that’s leaving Sardinia now or is most of it staying there?

ML

Most of it right now is staying there. There’s a pact of like twenty-five winemakers that created the group inside the Mamoiada, which is the region, and then they made a group called the Mamoja, which is a group of twenty-five. They’re only gonna work on Grenache, which is Cannonau in that region, and a native white varietal called Granatza, which is not related to Grenache, even though it sounds like it would be. 

RG

So for people who are familiar with Grenache, how is what they’re doing, you know, different than what you might, you know from Spain or know, even Australia?

ML

You know, here’s the thing. I don’t think it’s that much different from Spain and Australia, where if you go to drink Cannonau in Sardinia, it really is a little different than you know, Spanish Grenache and what you would find in Australia. So what they’re doing, from what it seems like and from talking with them, is really to chase these really great styles that Spain is. Comando G is probably the one of the hottest Grenache wines right now in maybe all the world. And same thing with like the Adelaides in Australia. They’re making like these leaner, fresh, precise styles that are crazy aromatic. And when I say crazy aromatic, I mean like they’re really enticing. They’re really I don’t want to say Burgundian, that’s an easy thing to say. I think that word’s thrown around so much, right? What does Burgundian even mean anymore? But they’re interesting aromatics that really grab the attention of a wine drinker.

RG

So if I was looking for some of these in the U.S., the ones that do make it here, what’s a producer I should be looking for?

ML

You know, there are very few right now in the U.S. The one that I’ve seemed to fall in love with is Vike Vike,  not just because I became close with the guy making the wine, I became close with the guy making the wine because I love his wines, you know? So I kinda had the wine first and then I found the guy. You know, it was one of those stories: I have to find the person that made this wine.

And how I had that wine is funny. I was in Cagliari, which is like a coastal town in Sardinia, me and my girlfriend were going out to dinner, but we had some time before, and we found some really cool historic wine shop and I saw all these Mamoja wines. And at the time I only knew one, and there was this one, Vike Vike, that stood out to me and I was like, that looks cool.

So we bought a bottle of the rosé and we actually just drank it out of the bottle on the way to dinner. And out of the bottle without a wine glass, we were like, wow, this is pretty good. So after that, we started looking all over town for wines. And because you’re in Sardinia, we had access to almost all of them.

RG

The winemaking process, what’s it like in the vineyard? A lot of these are biodynamic, are they organic wineries?

ML

Yeah, these are as raw as it comes, which is really great. You know, it’s such a small region, such a small production at the moment. and they’re just raw wines, you know. They’re pretty much stainless steel focused in the beginning of their winemaking, and then it sees time in oak for you know just resting and aging. But because of that stainless steel fermentation, you are getting a lot of freshness on the nose and on the palate. 

The whole vine system is like bush-trained vines, right? Really sitting low to the ground. They get wind constantly up in that mountainous region because they’re kind of pressed to the east coast and high altitude. So that low-trained vine system is pretty much needed unless they find like a little valley or something that they could plant new vines, which some people have been doing. They also started putting zones on their labels. So there’s a north, there’s an east, a south, a west, and they are distinguishing how different these are, which they are different, just like any other AOC or DOC or DOCG would tell you. It’s a very different composition for each vineyard.

RG

But it’s not a DOC or is it? No, it’s not.

ML

No, it’s not. So this is what’s funny about it, and I really like it. The Mamoja, they’re kind of rebellious, and I think that’s a very important thing in winemaking, right? The DOC for Cannonau di Sardinia is the whole island of Sardinia. Which is kind of crazy, right? Like that really falls into IGT category, if you look anywhere else in Italy.

RG

Yeah.

ML

If you look at a zone that big, it kind of falls into IGT category. So what they’re doing is kind of saying, We don’t want to be a part of that DOC because we’re small, so we should be a DOC. So they’re purposely declassifying it for that reason, and that is why they came up with the group, the Mamoja, because they believe in something new and different.

RG

So in the future they hope to one day have their own?

ML

Yeah, I mean that was a question I brought up with the winemakers. Like, do you want to be a DOC? And some of them say, Yeah, we would like that ’cause we wanna be recognized, but other people right now are enjoying that kind of rebellious nature. It’s kinda drawing attention, which normally, you know, those acts do, you know, they draw attention to people and they’re doing a good job at it.

RG

Yeah, and they kinda just enjoy the complete lack of guardrails. So if they were of a DOC then there’d be other restrictions that would then come about, right?

ML

For sure. Yeah, they would have to put all their and they have rules that they set for themselves inside their own group of twenty five winemakers, which I think is really great, you know. And if you look in the history of winemaking, anytime somebody makes a group or calls themselves a group, really great things happen. I mean, because we’re in Italy, I think the most obvious one is the Barolo boys, right?

RG

Yeah.

ML

So they they started getting away from like that austere, big, powerful, which of course Barolo is still powerful, but that that again, that old man stuff that you have to wait for to become a beautiful wine. Another one could be the Gang of Four, for Beaujolais, which really put natural winemaking practices out into the world.

You know, and they all created groups for themselves to become recognized and become a little rebellious and you know, it was really great.

RG

How are they all working together? Are they sharing fruit? Is it kind of like a co-op?

ML

No, they all have their own vineyards. Yeah, it’s not a co-op. No one’s making wine together or sharing wine. They have vineyards that go back with vine age that are the oldest I found were around eighty-five years old. And then some other people are just finding new places to plant vineyards and they’re not ready yet. 

RG

They all do.

ML

Mamoiada always had vines and there are still some you know old styles that exist there. Yeah, like you know, Montisci which is probably the most historic one, he’s actually in the zone where all these guys are making wine for the Mamoja. And it’s funny, this guy refuses to talk to them really because he thinks that they’re going against the traditional style, which they absolutely are, but in my opinion they’re making better wine for what the world is asking for at the moment.

And not just at the moment. I think these styles of wine are a little bit more with more longevity, you know what I mean? Like think of Burgundy. People love those styles of wine and that’s kinda where we’re going. Like a little lean, fresh, maybe a little bit of tannin, right? But nothing that’s too big and bold and in your face, you know. These are wines that are fun, easy to drink, but l like I said, they’re a lot more exciting and a lot more accessible to drink at the moment. You know, you don’t have to wait a couple years, you can pull the cork now and see what’s in that bottle.

RG

What are the biggest flavors? Like cherry flavors, strawberry, what are we dealing with?

ML

It varies across the board. I would say yeah, you’re definitely getting like a leaner-style cherry flavor. Nothing like black cherry or dark cherry like that. Nothing overripe cherry either. 

Could there be strawberry or those red fruits? Absolutely. I don’t think you’re getting anything that’s gonna be like tart berry or like, you know, like kind of like a bramble berry-type thing or a raspberry or something like that. You’re you’re in the roasted lean fresh cherry world. They’re crushable, but they’re also refined, you know. 

So for me, listen, I get to drink really great wines, you know, and sometimes they are very expensive. I’m not buying them, though, you know what I mean? Not yet in my life, anyway. Hopefully one day I could point at a bottle of DRC and buy it. but that’s not happening, and these wines are falling in that category of price right now where they’re not cheap, but they’re also not expensive. So you could find on a wine list at around like a hundred and thirty to hundred and fifty dollars, where that’s pretty much my price point if I’m looking for a really good bottle of wine.

RG

In the shop, what would they be?

ML

In the shop, you’d probably find them around forty five to fifty dollars, ranging all the way up to around ninety dollars for their high-end Ghirada, which is what they call their cru or their contrada.

RG

And what what’s the white like? What’s the white called again? Yeah, what’s that like?

ML

The white’s Granatza. It’s actually really, really interesting. They could resemble things like Chenin. They could also resemble not burgundy, but they have a little reduction to them like you would find in Burgundy, right? And when I say reduction, just these aromatics that are a little bit more, I don’t know, the best way to say for someone that doesn’t know reduction that are different. 

There’s no oxidative thing happening here, like brown apple type stuff or like applesauce type stuff. But there’s a beautiful reduction on these wines that again, if you’re a serious wine drinker and really into wine, Sardinian Granatza’s really what you want in that category. Yeah they’re they’re pretty high end. They’re cool. And the whole winemaking process there changed a lot because there’s one specific winemaker from a winery called Esole. She went away to the Loire, started making Chenin, and she found some practices there on vine training that was super important for the wine. One thing is like how you arc the vine instead of like you could actually take a vine and just bend it ninety, right? And what you’re doing there is you’re kinda constricting let’s just say flow through the vine, where the arc is actually like you’re you’re kind of forcing a little bit more harder travel, but it’s actually more fluent. And it just a little bit more precision inside the the final juice, you know? That’s something that she learned and brought over to the Mamoja from France.

RG

Well, I think I think we covered it. I could keep talking about Sardinia all day, but I think we gotta wrap it up, man.

ML

Yeah, man. I could talk about it too. It’s something I fell in love with. I fell in love with the region first just for visiting. And then by, you know, by natural discovery, I found these wines and to me I think they’re the most exciting wines right now in Italy. Because it’s a style that you really haven’t seen in Italy yet, and it’s happening in Sardinia, which is pretty cool.

RG

Yeah, I would love some more to make it over here.

ML

Yeah, for sure, man. Well, I appreciate you having me here, man. And anytime you want to talk Italian wine and shop, I’m here for you, brother.

RG

That sounds great. Thanks for hopping on.

RG

And that about does it for this episode. We have three fascinating Italian regions that really should be on your radar if they aren’t already. Check out more from Italy in the 2026 Italy issue in print and online at wineenthusiast.com. Send us your comments and questions at podcast@ wineenthusiast.com. Subscribe to this podcast on Apple, Spotify, and anywhere else you listen to your favorite shows. You can also go to wineenthusiast.com/podcast for more episodes and transcripts. I’m Ryan Grim, thanks for listening.

Designed to Shine: The Italian Prosecco That Doubles as a Statement Piece

Whether you’re planning a milestone celebration or simply gathering a small group of friends for an impromptu dinner party, the details can feel overwhelming. There’s a menu to set, a table to shape, a guest list to curate, and, of course, drinks to pour.

Choosing a bottle that looks like it belongs at the table adds to that convivial feeling, which is why Brilla!, premium Italian Prosecco is the preferred choice for so many hosts.

Combining authentic Italian craftsmanship with modern style, Brilla! Prosecco DOC Rosé and Prosecco DOC are an effortless choice to pair alongside classic entertaining fare, from freshly shucked oysters to shrimp cocktail to charcuterie. 

With a delicate and complex bouquet of pear, green apple, and lemon as well as floral notes of acacia and rose, the Rosé is fresh and light on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

Made from Prosecco’s iconic white grape, Glera, known for producing light-bodied, high-acid wines with neutral to fruit-forward aromatics, along with Pinot Noir, the blend offers a round and full-bodied structure. This makes it perfect to enjoy as an aperitif, but also positions it as an ideal accompaniment to Prosciutto e Melone (Cured Ham & Cantaloupe) and grilled fish entrées.

Meanwhile, the crisp and dry profile of the Prosecco DOC feels fresh on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

The pronounced peach and green apple notes set the tone for a decadent evening of al fresco summer dinners and pair impeccably with seasonal favorites likegrilled chicken and peaches. And the iconic sound of popping open a bottle only prolongs guests’ desire to linger at the table for hours, talking long after the meal is complete. 

Don’t be surprised if Brilla!’s distinctive, jewel-inspired bottle design comes up as a topic. The conversation-starting, covetable object reflects the meaning of the Italian word (“to shine”). It’s the ideal choice for hosts who understand that the eyes eat first, and that the style of a tablescape influences how guests feel about the menu, the company, and the celebration to come. 

“Brilla was designed to stand apart long before the first pour,” says a representative from the brand. “Its distinctive patented textured bottle, inspired by the brilliance of cut crystal, transforms every bottle into a statement piece—reflecting the sparkle, elegance, and celebration found inside.”

The Brilla! bottle is the result of a design study that goes beyond a simple wine bottle. Its patented texture is reminiscent of a diamond, and echoes a classic gemstone drop shape.

In the world of diamonds, drop-shaped stones are among the most distinctive and difficult to craft; the symmetry, which is achieved with hard work and dedication during processing, is key to the overall beauty of this stone.

Worn as a ring, earring, or pendant, the shape provides a characteristic elegance with which no other diamond cut can compete; it enhances, romantically and gently, the wearer’s form.

This makes each bottle an effortless gift, requiring no additional gift wrap or presentation.

As a natural bridge between the worlds of fashion, design, and hospitality, Brilla! is a beloved choice for making celebratory, Prosecco-based cocktails, which can signal the start of a brunch or aperitif hour in style.

Some of the most common and popular examples include the Aperol Spritz, Bellini, Mimosa, and Negroni Sbagliato, with Prosecco.

In each of these cocktails, Brilla! adds a layer of sophistication and complexity, and sets the tone for an elevated, elegant occasion that guests will associate with a design-minded host.
